Q: How can I get a source code of Python function which was declared by using 'exec' inside other function? A:

There are two errors in your code:

  1. the combination of exec & locals
  2. the OSError: could not get source code generated by inspect

Error 1 is related on implementation and optimisation details of exec and locals:

  1. A. from the doc of exec

Note The default locals act as described for function locals() below. Pass an explicit locals dictionary if you need to see effects of the code on locals after function exec() returns.

  1. B. from the doc of locals

In an optimized scope (including functions, generators, and coroutines), each call to locals() instead returns a fresh dictionary containing the current bindings of the function's local variables and any nonlocal cell references. In this case, name binding changes made via the returned dict are not written back to the corresponding local variables [...] and assigning, reassigning, or deleting local variables and nonlocal cell references does not affect the contents of previously returned dictionaries.

To fix error 1 the code should be smt like

def declare_func():
    func_code=\
'''def new_func():
    print("Hello, world!")'''
    scope = {}
    exec(func_code, None, locals=scope)
    return scope['new_func'] # or scope.pop()

This will still raise error 2.

To fix error 2 you should fake inspect.getsource which is complaining about the missing file where the function should be declared. Let investigate the previous the monkey-patched function

f = declare_func()

print(f.__code__.co_filename)    # print: <string>
print(f.__code__.co_firstlineno) # print: 1

so the function is not physically defined in a file and bypass it use the linecache package from the standard library. Let's reimplement the previous function by adding the fake-file definition

import linecache

def declare_func():
    func_code=\
'''def new_func():
    print("Hello, world!")'''

    fake_filename = "<monkey_string>"
    linecache.cache[fake_filename] = (
        len(func_code),
        None,
        [line + '\n' for line in func_code.splitlines()],
        fake_filename
    )
    
    compiled_code = compile(func_code, fake_filename, 'exec')
    scope = {}
    exec(compiled_code, None, scope)

    return scope['new_func']

print(f.__code__.co_filename)     # Print: <monkey_string>
print(f.__code__.co_firstlineno)   # 1

and do the final check

from inspect import getsource

print(getsource(f))

which output

def new_func():
    print("Hello, world!")

Q: How to get coordinates of all vertical lines using OpenCV A:

Here is a different approach to the solution in Python OpenCV.

  • Read the input

  • Threshold on white

  • Get Canny edges

  • Get the edge coordinates of the first row. Edges should come in pairs corresponding to the sides of the stripes.

  • Print the list of x,y edge coordinates

  • Get the center x coordinate between each pair of edges.

  • Print the list of center x coordinates

  • Save results

Input image:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# read the input
img = cv2.imread('stripes.png')
hh, ww = img.shape[:2]

# Threshold on white
low = (255,255,255)
high = (255,255,255)
thresh = cv2.inRange(img, low, high)

# get edges
# note: edges will be in pairs
edges = cv2.Canny(thresh, 100, 200)

# get edge coordinates from first row
# note: coords will be y,x from numpy
print("\n ---Coordinates of Lines ---")
coords = np.column_stack(np.where(edges[0:1, 0:ww] == 255))
num_coords = len(coords)
print(coords)

# test for complete pairs
if (num_coords % 2) != 0:
    print('\n--- Error: Unpaired Lines ---')
    exit()

# get center between pair of points
print("\n--- X Centers of Stripes ---")
for curr_coord, next_coord in zip(coords, coords[1:]):
    y1, x1 = curr_coord
    y2, x2 = next_coord
    
    # Calculate the center x value between the pair
    center_x = (x1 + x2) / 2
    
    print(f"X = {center_x}")

# save images
cv2.imwrite('sripes_thresh.png', thresh)
cv2.imwrite('stripes_edges.png', edges)

# show the images
cv2.imshow('thresh', thresh)
cv2.imshow('edges', edges)
cv2.waitKey(0)

Q: Jira Rest api V2: user search is not working with pagination A:

It's not a like-for-like replacement but if you're stuck with an on-prem Jira and want to enumerate all users (no filtering required) then there is /rest/api/2/user/list (docs) as mentioned on https://jira.atlassian.com/browse/JRASERVER-78660

Q: How to receive response from ActivityCompat.requestPermissions running in Adobe Native Extension (ANE) context? A:

As mentioned in this discussion, it is not possible to override or add methods at runtime to another class, in this case main AIR app activity. So probably the best way is to launch a new blank Activity for the purpose of triggering the popup and so be able to wait for the onRequestPermissionsResult() response.

I managed to get own working basic ANE version, which is opensourced here: https://github.com/Oldes/ANEAmanitaAndroid-public/tree/eclipse-permissions

Q: What is the optimized regex to match the email pattern in java A:

The slowdown is mainly caused by backtracking. With a very long string that doesn’t contain a valid email, the regex engine can end up trying many different ways to match the repeated parts before finally failing.

One simple improvement is to make the repeated sections possessive where possible, for example:

[a-z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]++

Possessive quantifiers prevent the engine from backtracking over characters it has already consumed.

That said, if you’re scanning large arbitrary text for an email address, I wouldn’t rely on one large regex for the whole job. It can be more efficient to first locate candidates containing @ and then apply the email validation regex to those smaller pieces. This avoids making the regex engine process a huge block of irrelevant text.
